title: 2022 wiretapping scandal: EYP surveillance of Nikos Androulakis and Predator spyware
description: In July 2022 PASOK leader Nikos Androulakis, then an MEP, revealed that European Parliament services had detected an attempt to infect his phone with the Predator spyware, and it emerged that the National Intelligence Service (EYP) had placed his phone under surveillance from September 2021. Mitsotakis had placed EYP under the direct authority of the Prime Minister's office in 2019 (Law 4622/2019). On 5 August 2022 his General Secretary and nephew Grigoris Dimitriadis and EYP chief Panagiotis Kontoleon resigned; the government maintained the EYP surveillance was legal, with a prosecutor's order, and denied any link to Predator. In a televised address on 8 August 2022 Mitsotakis said the surveillance 'might have been in accordance with the letter of the law, but it was wrong', that he had not known about it and that it was 'politically unacceptable'. Opposition parties blamed him directly. In February 2024 the European Parliament asked Greece to reverse the legislation placing the intelligence service under the Prime Minister. On 26 February 2026 the Athens single-member misdemeanour court convicted four people linked to the Predator vendor Intellexa (Tal Dilian, Sara Hamou, Felix Bitzios and Giannis Lavranos) of offences including violation of the secrecy of communications against 87 victims, with sentences suspended pending appeal, and sent the file to prosecutors for further investigation. In an act dated 27 April 2026 Supreme Court Prosecutor Konstantinos Tzavellas declined to reopen the archived investigation, reaffirming that no state agency, including EYP, had been found to be involved with Predator. Mitsotakis is not a party to these proceedings.
key_facts: EYP placed under the Prime Minister's office after the 2019 election
5 August 2022: Dimitriadis and Kontoleon resigned
8 August 2022: Mitsotakis said the surveillance was legal but wrong and that he had not known
26 February 2026: four Intellexa-linked defendants convicted at first instance (misdemeanours, sentences suspended pending appeal)
27 April 2026: Supreme Court Prosecutor refused to reopen the archived case; no state agency found to be involved
Mitsotakis is not a party to any of the proceedings

title: Tempi rail disaster (2023): handling of the aftermath and cover-up allegations
description: On 28 February 2023 a passenger train from Athens to Thessaloniki collided head-on with a freight train near Tempi; 57 people died. Transport Minister Kostas A. Karamanlis resigned. Victims' relatives and the opposition accused the government of failing to fix the railway and of covering up evidence, notably the clearing ('backfilling') of the crash site in the days after the collision. Parliament rejected no-confidence motions over the disaster in March 2024 (159–141) and on 7 March 2025 (157–136); the second followed protests of more than 300,000 people across Greece on the second anniversary, and a report by the state accident investigation agency (HARSIA) pointing to the 'possible presence' of an unknown fuel. Mitsotakis told parliament that 'there never was' a cover-up and called the claims a 'colourful collection of myths, fantasies and lies'. Deputy Minister Christos Triantopoulos, whom Mitsotakis had sent to the site, resigned in February 2025; in September 2026 the Judicial Council referred him and four officials to the Special Court for ministerial responsibility on a misdemeanour charge of breach of duty. In July 2025 parliament voted by secret ballot (157 to 6) to refer Karamanlis to the Judicial Council for possible breach of duty. The criminal trial of 36 defendants, mostly railway staff and officials, opened in Larissa on 23 March 2026. Mitsotakis is not a defendant in these proceedings; criminal complaints that name him are listed in the justice section.
key_facts: 57 dead on 28 February 2023, Greece's deadliest rail disaster
No-confidence motions defeated in March 2024 and March 2025
HARSIA investigation report published in 2025 (Greek version 23 May 2025)
Triantopoulos referred to the Special Court (September 2026); Karamanlis referred to the Judicial Council by parliament (July 2025)
Trial of 36 defendants opened in Larissa on 23 March 2026

title: OPEKEPE farm-subsidy fraud investigated by the European Public Prosecutor's Office
description: The European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) is investigating an alleged organised fraud scheme involving EU agricultural funds and corruption at OPEKEPE, the Greek agency paying Common Agricultural Policy subsidies: beneficiaries allegedly claimed land and livestock they did not own, with Greek authorities estimating about €23 million in fraudulent payments since around 2018. According to DW, most of the suspect subsidies went to Crete, where Mitsotakis's family has long held political sway. On 19 June 2025 the EPPO referred to parliament information on two former Ministers of Rural Development, stating that the Greek Constitution (Article 86) prevents it from investigating serving or former members of the government and that it had reported this as a breach of the EPPO regulation to the European Commission. Five senior officials stepped down in 2025; on 3 April 2026 Mitsotakis replaced Agriculture Minister Kostas Tsiaras, Civil Protection Minister Yiannis Kefalogiannis and Deputy Health Minister Dimitris Vartzopoulos, who resigned while denying wrongdoing, and appointed former European Commission Vice-President Margaritis Schinas as agriculture minister. Mitsotakis has vowed to imprison the 'thieves' responsible and recover the money. In April 2026 parliament lifted the immunity of 11 sitting MPs at the EPPO's request; according to To Vima, the EPPO later charged 22 people, including four sitting MPs (Katerina Papakosta, Kostas Skrekas, Christos Boukoros and Maximos Senetakis), and closed the case against seven others, including Tsiaras, Kefalogiannis and Vartzopoulos, for lack of evidence. Those charged are presumed innocent. Mitsotakis is not a party to the investigation.
key_facts: EPPO investigation into OPEKEPE subsidy fraud; about €23 million in suspect payments since 2018 per Greek authorities
19 June 2025: EPPO referred information on two former ministers to parliament under Article 86
3 April 2026: two ministers and a deputy minister resigned, denying wrongdoing; Margaritis Schinas appointed agriculture minister
22 people charged, including four sitting MPs; case closed for seven MPs for lack of evidence
Mitsotakis is not a party

title: Migration: pushback allegations and the 2025 suspension of asylum claims
description: Since 2019 Mitsotakis's government has built a fence on the northern land border and stepped up sea patrols (Al Jazeera). Rights groups and journalists have accused Greek authorities of illegal pushbacks of migrants, which the government denies. On 7 January 2025 the European Court of Human Rights ruled in A.R.E. v. Greece that Greece had violated Articles 3, 5 and 13 of the Convention by returning a Turkish asylum seeker across the Evros river without examining her claim, and pointed to evidence of a broader systematic practice of pushbacks. In July 2025, after about 2,000 people landed on Crete in a few days, Mitsotakis announced in parliament that Greece would suspend the examination of asylum applications for people arriving by sea from North Africa, initially for three months; parliament approved the measure by 177 votes to 74, over objections from the UNHCR and the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, and a left-wing challenge that it was unconstitutional failed.
key_facts: ECtHR, A.R.E. v. Greece (7 January 2025): violations of Articles 3, 5 and 13; evidence of a systematic practice of pushbacks
July 2025: three-month suspension of asylum claims for sea arrivals from North Africa, adopted 177–74
The government denies carrying out pushbacks

title: European Parliament resolution on the rule of law and media freedom in Greece (2024)
description: On 7 February 2024 the European Parliament adopted, by 330 votes to 254 with 26 abstentions, a resolution expressing 'severe concerns about very serious threats to democracy, the rule of law and fundamental rights in Greece'. It cited the distribution of state funds to media outlets, the use of spyware against journalists and politicians, the lack of progress in the investigation of the 2021 murder of journalist Giorgos Karaivaz, the independence of oversight bodies, and called for the reversal of the law placing the intelligence service under the Prime Minister. The text adopted in plenary was tabled by the S&D, Renew, Greens/EFA and Left groups. The EU criminal-law journal eucrim noted Greece's low ranking in the World Press Freedom Index in its summary of the resolution.
key_facts: Adopted 7 February 2024 by 330–254, 26 abstentions
Concerns over media funding, spyware, the Karaivaz murder investigation and the independence of oversight bodies
Called for reversing the placement of the intelligence service under the Prime Minister

title: Leak of diaspora voters' data used for ND campaign emails (2023–2024)
description: On 1 March 2024 ND MEP Anna-Michelle Asimakopoulou sent an unsolicited campaign email to Greek voters abroad. The Hellenic Data Protection Authority found that a Ministry of the Interior file with the contact details of all registered expatriate voters for the June 2023 elections had leaked between 8 and 23 June 2023 and had been passed on 23 June 2023, by an unidentified sender, to ND's then Secretary for Greeks Abroad, who sent it to Asimakopoulou in January 2024. In May 2024 the authority fined the Interior Ministry €400,000 and Asimakopoulou €40,000; in October 2024 it fined ND €40,000 and two party officials €10,000 each, saying more than 25,000 diaspora Greeks were affected. Asimakopoulou withdrew from the European election; ND said it would appeal to the Council of State. Mitsotakis is not personally a party to the decisions.
key_facts: Interior Ministry file leaked in June 2023 and reached ND's diaspora secretary
May 2024: €400,000 fine on the Interior Ministry and €40,000 on Asimakopoulou
October 2024: €40,000 fine on ND and €10,000 on each of two party officials; ND appeal announced

title: Ikaria lunch during COVID-19 restrictions (2021)
description: During a visit to Ikaria on 6 February 2021 to inspect COVID-19 vaccinations, Mitsotakis was filmed at a lunch with about thirty guests on the balcony of the house of Christodoulos Stefanadis, a doctor and local ND MP, a day after the government had tightened restrictions, including a ban on home gatherings; Euronews reported it as the second accusation in three months that he had broken his government's COVID-19 rules. Government spokesperson Christos Tarantilis said the Prime Minister had stayed for 'a snack and a short meal' and called the criticism inaccurate. Mitsotakis later said the images had hurt people, did not reflect his intentions and would not happen again.
key_facts: Lunch with about 30 people on 6 February 2021
Second accusation of breaching COVID-19 rules after December 2020
Mitsotakis said it would not happen again

title: Expulsion of former Prime Minister Antonis Samaras from New Democracy (2024)
description: On 16 November 2024 the government announced that former Prime Minister Antonis Samaras had been expelled from ND after he called in a To Vima interview for Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis to be removed over the 'calm waters' talks with Turkey. Government spokesman Pavlos Marinakis said Samaras had expressed 'total disagreement with the whole of the current government policy' and had 'adopted extreme lies, distorting statements by the Foreign Minister'. Samaras, who had also criticised the government for what he called a 'woke' agenda on social matters, said his expulsion resulted from 'arrogance and an obvious lack of composure' on Mitsotakis's part (AFP).
key_facts: 16 November 2024: expulsion announced by the government spokesman
Trigger: Samaras's call to dismiss the foreign minister over Greek-Turkish talks
Samaras attributed the expulsion to Mitsotakis's 'arrogance and an obvious lack of composure'

title: Public-sector 'mobility' scheme and job cuts as reform minister (2013–2015)
description: As Minister of Administrative Reform and e-Governance in Antonis Samaras's government, Mitsotakis responded to the debt crisis and bailout by reorganising government institutions and overseeing what Britannica describes as dramatic reductions in the public-service workforce and the restructuring of the tax administration. According to Greek Wikipedia, he oversaw a 'mobility' (κινητικότητα) programme for 12,000 civil servants that led to the removal of the Finance Ministry's cleaners and of hundreds of school guards, while municipal police officers and university administrative staff were moved to other posts.
key_facts: Minister from June 2013 to January 2015
Mobility scheme for about 12,000 civil servants (Greek Wikipedia)
Dismissals of ministry cleaners and school guards
